youtube.title: First Blood Transfusion: Why Did Some Live and Others Die?
youtube.description:
The first blood transfusion experiments began in 1667, when a Paris doctor put the blood of a lamb, then a calf, into human veins. Some patients lived. Many did not, and nobody knew why for more than two hundred years.

Jean-Baptiste Denys, a physician to Louis XIV, gave lamb's blood to a feverish fifteen-year-old boy, then tried calf's blood on Antoine Mauroy, a man with fits of madness. Mauroy's urine turned black, he later died, and the case ended in a Paris court with arsenic, a suspected wife and a ruling that stopped transfusion for about 150 years. James Blundell brought it back in London with human blood, and Karl Landsteiner finally found the answer in Vienna in 1901: blood groups.

In this video:
- Harvey's circle and Richard Lower's dogs in Oxford
- The boy and the lamb, Paris, June 1667
- The madman, the calf and the black urine
- Arsenic, a trial and the 1668 ruling
- Blundell's gamble with human blood in London
- Landsteiner's red knots and the first blood bank

Subscribe to Stickstory for more true stories of the human body. Would you have let a doctor try this in 1667? Tell me in the comments!

scenes.text: Paris, at the end of 1667. A man lies in a candlelit room, and beside him a calf is tied down.
scenes.visual: Night interior, stone wall: a dark window, a candle in the foreground; a man asleep in a wooden bed paints in, then a calf lying tied on the floor beside it; note 'Paris, 1667'.

scenes.text: A thin tube carries the animal's blood into his arm. His doctors hope a gentle animal's blood will cure his madness.
scenes.visual: Closer on the same candlelit room: a thin silver tube runs from the calf's neck to the man's arm, and on 'blood' it fills red from the calf toward the arm. From 'hope' a faint red warmth gathers over his arm where the tube goes in.

scenes.text: Within minutes, his arm begins to burn.
scenes.visual: Close-up plate on clean paper: the crook of a bare arm above a rolled white cuff, the silver tube entering the vein already full of red; on 'arm' a hot red glow swells around it; note 'burning'.

scenes.text: The next morning, his urine is as black as chimney soot.
scenes.visual: An aged sheet written in line by line: Denys's own words, 'as black as if it had been mixed with the soot of chimneys', signed 'J.-B. Denys, 1668'.

lines: as if it had been mixed

scenes.text: Some of the first people to receive blood survived. Many did not. But it would take more than two hundred years to learn why.
scenes.visual: One big painted number '200+' on a gold swatch, hand note 'years to learn why'.

scenes.text: For most of history, doctors did not give blood. They took it. Sick patients were bled to restore the balance of the body's fluids.
scenes.visual: Specimen plate: a pewter bleeding bowl full of blood with a lancet beside it; notes 'bloodletting' and 'the lancet'.

scenes.text: Then, in 1628, William Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood around the body in a closed circle.
scenes.visual: An anatomical heart painted large with its great vessels; a red ring of three arrows circles it; notes 'William Harvey, 1628' and 'a closed circle'.

scenes.text: That opened a door. If blood travels in a circle, perhaps it could be moved from one body into another.
scenes.visual: A plate on clean paper: the silver transfusion tube painted large, a quill joint at one end, a red drop at the tip, a thin red line inside; note 'one body to another?'.

scenes.text: In Oxford, in 1665, Richard Lower drained a dog almost to death and refilled it with another dog's blood. The dog lived. In Paris, an ambitious doctor wondered: could it work on a human?
scenes.visual: Map of southern England and northern France: Oxford marked with a star and 'Richard Lower, 1665'; on 'Paris' a red route crosses the Channel to Paris.

scenes.text: Jean-Baptiste Denys was a physician to King Louis the Fourteenth.
scenes.visual: Chapter card: 'Chapter 2 · The Boy and the Lamb · Paris, June 1667' with a small lamb lying down.

scenes.text: On the fifteenth of June, 1667, he was called to a fifteen-year-old boy who had burned with fever for two months.
scenes.visual: A Paris street on a summer day: half-timbered and stone houses on both sides, a spire beyond; a physician in a cape and plumed hat walks down it; note '15 June 1667'.

scenes.text: Bled about twenty times, the boy could barely stay awake.
scenes.visual: Close on the pale boy asleep on his pillow, a bleeding bowl full of blood on the floor by the bed; note 'bled 20 times'.

scenes.text: Denys decided to put blood back in, but not human blood. He chose a lamb, the purest animal he could think of.
scenes.visual: Specimen plate: a white lamb lying down, painted large on clean paper; notes 'the purest animal' and 'not human blood'.

scenes.text: About twelve ounces went into the boy's arm, and the next morning he was alert.
scenes.visual: A big painted '12' on a red swatch, hand note 'ounces of lamb's blood', smaller note 'alert next morning'.

scenes.text: It looked like a miracle. Soon all of Paris was talking about Denys. But that fame led him to his most dangerous patient.
scenes.visual: A Paris street at dusk between lit houses: a knot of townspeople gathered talking; note 'the talk of Paris'.

scenes.text: Antoine Mauroy was thirty-four, and he suffered from fits of madness.
scenes.visual: Chapter card: 'Chapter 3 · The Madman and the Calf · Paris, winter 1667' with a small calf lying down.

scenes.text: Denys and his patrons had a bold idea. If a calm animal's blood flowed into a troubled man, perhaps it would calm him too.
scenes.visual: A study at night: a writing desk with an open book, a quill in its ink pot and a candle; note 'calm blood, calm mind?'.

scenes.text: So they chose a calf. The first time, only five or six ounces got through, and afterwards Mauroy seemed quieter.
scenes.visual: Winter night, the candlelit room again: Mauroy in the bed, the calf tied on the floor, the tube between them filling red on 'five'; note '5 or 6 ounces'.

scenes.text: When they tried again, his body fought back. His pulse raced, his back ached, and he felt as if he would choke.
scenes.visual: Denys's account of the second transfusion written in line by line: 'a great heat along his arm · his pulse rising · pains in his kidneys · as if ready to choke', signed 'Denys's account, 1667'.

lines: a great heat along his arm

scenes.text: Then came the black urine. His body was treating the calf's blood as an invader, destroying it cell by cell, and the wreckage poured out through his kidneys.
scenes.visual: A brass magnifying lens on the paper: red human cells and paler calf cells drift in the liquid; on 'destroying' the calf cells break up into dark specks that sink away; notes 'calf cells' and 'destroyed'.

scenes.text: Yet Mauroy recovered and went home to his wife, Perrine.
scenes.visual: A quiet Paris lane on a grey winter morning: a man and a woman walk side by side toward a small house; note 'home'.

scenes.text: Months later his madness returned, and Perrine begged Denys to try once more.
scenes.visual: Night interior: Perrine, hands clasped, pleading before the physician in his cape by a candle; note 'once more'.

scenes.text: The attempt was barely under way when Mauroy shook in a violent fit. The next day, he was dead. So was it the blood?
scenes.visual: The candlelit room with the bed and the calf, the tube only half-laid; on 'dead' the whole picture washes slowly back into paper; note 'the blood?'.

scenes.text: Perrine blamed Denys, and the case went to court.
scenes.visual: The Grand Châtelet, Paris's fortress court: a gate between two round towers under a grey sky; note 'Grand Châtelet'.

scenes.text: Then investigators found something no one expected. Arsenic.
scenes.visual: A small glass flask alone on the plate, a white powder inside; on 'Arsenic' a red note 'arsenic'.

scenes.text: The court decided that poison, not calf's blood, had killed Mauroy. Some said his wife had slipped it into his broth.
scenes.visual: A plain kitchen table by a window: a plain bowl of broth and the little flask beside it, a candle; note 'in his broth?'.

scenes.text: Others believed Denys's rivals had paid her to blame him. Denys walked free.
scenes.visual: A gold coin painted large, slowly turning; note 'paid to blame him?'.

scenes.text: But in April 1668, the court added a rule. No transfusion on any human body without the approval of the Paris Faculty of Medicine, and the Faculty wanted nothing to do with it.
scenes.visual: The court's ruling on old paper, written in line by line: 'No transfusion upon any human body without the approval of the Faculty of Medicine.' signed 'Paris court, 17 April 1668'.

scenes.text: Transfusion stopped. For about a hundred and fifty years, almost nobody dared to try again.
scenes.visual: One big painted number '150' on a red swatch, hand note 'years of silence'.

scenes.text: The silence ended in London.
scenes.visual: Chapter card: 'Chapter 5 · A Gamble in London · 1818 – 1829' with a small candle.

scenes.text: The obstetrician James Blundell kept watching women bleed to death after giving birth.
scenes.visual: London in rain: a brick hospital with many windows, St Paul's-like dome far away; a doctor in a dark coat and hat stands outside; note 'James Blundell'.

scenes.text: His experiments on dogs showed what Denys had missed: blood from another species was dangerous.
scenes.visual: A bare laboratory floor: a dog lying on one side, a lamb on the other, a tube between them; on 'another' a red note 'another species: danger'.

scenes.text: So the blood had to come from a human. In 1829 he reported a mother, bleeding after childbirth, who received about eight ounces from his assistant.
scenes.visual: A London lying-in room, pale walls and a pointed window: the mother in bed, head to the right; the assistant stands right beside the bed and a tube runs from his arm to hers, filling red on 'eight'; note '8 ounces'.

scenes.text: She said it felt as if life were being poured into her body. She lived.
scenes.visual: Blundell's report in The Lancet, written in by hand: 'She felt as if life were infused into her body.' signed 'The Lancet, 1829'.

scenes.text: But across ten recorded attempts, success came only some of the time.
scenes.visual: One big painted number '10' on a blue swatch, hand note 'recorded attempts', smaller note 'only some lived'.

scenes.text: Same doctor, same method, same human blood, and still one patient lived while another died. Nobody could explain it.
scenes.visual: Two candles on clean paper: the left one burning, the right one just blown out with a curl of smoke; notes 'lived' and 'died' and a red 'why?'.

scenes.text: In 1900, in Vienna, Karl Landsteiner tried a simple experiment.
scenes.visual: Chapter card: 'Chapter 6 · Red Knots · Vienna, 1900' with a small rack of test tubes.

scenes.text: He took blood from his colleagues, separated the red cells from the clear liquid, and mixed them in every combination.
scenes.visual: A Vienna laboratory by a tall window: a desk with a brass microscope and a rack of test tubes, bookshelves behind; note 'cells + serum'.

scenes.text: Sometimes the mixture stayed smooth. Sometimes the cells clumped into tiny red knots.
scenes.visual: Under the brass lens: red cells drifting evenly in pale liquid; on 'clumped' they pull together into five tight red knots; note 'clumped'.

scenes.text: In 1901 he published the answer. Human blood comes in different groups.
scenes.visual: Specimen plate: the rack of four test tubes painted large, two smooth red, two clumped; notes 'smooth' and 'clumped' and 'groups'.

scenes.text: He called them A, B and C, the group we now call O. A year later, two colleagues found a fourth, AB.
scenes.visual: A short timeline painting itself in: 1901 'A, B, C', 'C = O', 1902 'AB'.

scenes.text: Suddenly the old mystery made sense. Blood attacks cells it does not recognise. A matching donor is safe, and the wrong one can kill.
scenes.visual: The lens again: red cells with a few paler strangers among them; on 'attacks' the strangers break apart into dark specks; notes 'match: safe' and 'wrong: deadly'.

scenes.text: Denys's first patients probably survived because very little animal blood reached them. Blundell's patients lived or died by the luck of the match. At first, almost nobody paid attention.
scenes.visual: Map of western Europe: Paris marked 'a few ounces', London marked 'luck of the match', Vienna with a red star.

scenes.text: That changed in New York in 1907, when Reuben Ottenberg tested a donor's blood against his patient's before a transfusion, the first one matched by type.
scenes.visual: Map of the American east coast: New York marked with a red star, 'Reuben Ottenberg, 1907' written in.

scenes.text: In 1930, Landsteiner won the Nobel Prize.
scenes.visual: A gold medal on a blue ribbon, a profile head in relief, painted large; note 'Nobel Prize, 1930'.

scenes.text: In 1937, in Chicago, Bernard Fantus opened a place where donated blood could be kept for days. He called it a blood bank.
scenes.visual: A modern blood bag painted large, red with a white label and its tube; notes 'Chicago, 1937' and 'blood bank'.

scenes.text: Today the fourteenth of June, Landsteiner's birthday, is World Blood Donor Day.
scenes.visual: A big painted date '14 June' on a red swatch, hand note 'World Blood Donor Day'.

scenes.text: Every bag of blood passed safely between strangers carries a little of this story, from a calf in a candlelit room to red knots in a glass tube.
scenes.visual: The whole story as a timeline painting itself in: 1628 Harvey's circle, 1667 the lamb and the calf, 1668 the ban, 1829 Blundell, 1901 blood groups, 1937 blood bank.
